motion: A booming China spells trouble for America.

dropped_turns.speaker: CON
dropped_turns.text: On the 'essential device part' point, the answer is diversification, not fearing growth. American businesses can develop backup suppliers and still benefit from Chinese customers.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Welcome to tonight's debate. Tonight's motion is whether a booming China spells trouble for America. Jacob argues for it, and Genevieve argues against it. Each speaker gets thirty seconds to open, followed by two and a half minutes of crossfire, then thirty-second closings; I will give a ten-second cue before time expires.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: A booming China does not merely offer new customers; it gives a rival government greater wealth, influence, and control over vital supply chains. When American jobs and essential goods depend on choices made elsewhere, prosperity becomes leverage. That leverage spells trouble for America. That's all, thank you.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Here's Genevieve to argue against whether a booming China spells trouble for America.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: A growing China can buy more from American makers. Prosperity is not fixed; when buyers and sellers gain, America can gain too, rather than treating...

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: But buying our goods can also build leverage-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Let her answer that, if you want to come back on this.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: it as harmless. If one buyer becomes powerful, American firms still have other customers and can set their own terms. More trade creates options, not automatic control.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten seconds please.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: That is why China's growth can expand American opportunity, not spell trouble.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: And that concludes round one. Now we move on to round two. And round two is where the debaters can address one another directly. Two and a half minutes on the clock, starting the moment I stop talking.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Imagine a Chinese supplier suddenly withholding key machine parts after a dispute. American workshops halt, workers lose pay, and choices shrink. That dependence proves booming Chinese power can trouble America.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Every Chinese success benefits America. How does a cheaper product from a growing China spell trouble when families save money and American sellers reach more customers?

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Cheaper goods do not erase the danger; I reject the idea that lower prices settle this. When vital production moves abroad, China gains leverage over American jobs, security, and choices.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: This Chinese success harms America. When a Chinese firm dominates a tool market, it can squeeze American rivals, yet overall growth still gives families more choices and lower costs.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: You're saying every Chinese success benefits America but you still want this Chinese success harms America.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Both statements fit: the same success harms America by exposing a weakness, while it benefits America through cheaper goods. The net effect remains opportunity, so China's growth is not trouble.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Your answer quietly swaps America for a single family at a checkout. Lower prices cannot compensate for lost capacity or coercion, so your claimed overall benefit ignores the motion's danger.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Take the tool market: machines need repair crews, spare bolts, training manuals, and warehouse schedules. Once a local workshop closes, its apprentices lose mentors, and the town's repair skills fade.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Okay. What does your point have to do with whether a booming China spells trouble for America?

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: That matters to the motion because China's growth need not cause those closures; American firms can adapt and sell into its expanding market. Trouble comes from poor domestic choices, not China's boom.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: No, I reject your claim that domestic choices alone explain closures. A giant competitor backed by its government can underprice rivals until supply chains rely on it, and then-

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: And then you assume competition is coercion. Firms can choose suppliers, build alternatives, and sell to Chinese customers; growth creates bargaining partners, not a command over America's future.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: If booming China gives its leaders more control over shipping and components, why should American workers trust that leverage will never be used against them?

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Your word 'never' is the weakness: no country can promise another government's future behavior. But fear of a possible abuse cannot make every Chinese success trouble for America.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: About ten seconds left in the crossfire.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Consider an American designer whose essential device part is made only in China. A political quarrel stops deliveries, customers wait, and the small business collapses. That proves concentrated power can-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Okay, time. Now we move on to round three. Round three will be closing statements. Here is Jacob.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Genevieve calls this diversification, but the motion asks what a booming China can do, not what we hope everyone will prevent. When its wealth turns into control over crucial goods and markets, American choices narrow. Cheap purchases today do not replace the independence lost when key businesses must wait for decisions made elsewhere.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Well, now ten.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: A boom that creates that leverage spells trouble, even if it also offers bargains. That's all, thank you.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Genevieve, the floor is yours.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: The strongest point is that growth creates more customers, more goods, and more American choice. A foreign boom is not a command over America; dependence results from America's own failures to adapt. Meet competition with resilience and trade, and China's prosperity becomes an opportunity, not trouble. That's all, thank you.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Thank you, Jacob and Genevieve, for a spirited exchange, and thank you for joining us for this debate.
